title: The Geometry Of The Gauss Map
notes: Open by framing the chapter as a way to turn surface bending into a map that can be measured on the unit sphere. The source span 136-219 introduces the normal field, its derivative, and the curvature invariants that make local surface geometry testable.

title: Chapter Route
notes: Use the route as a dependency graph. The unit normal gives the Gauss map, its differential becomes the shape operator, self-adjointness supplies principal directions, determinant and trace become curvatures, and examples plus diagnostics teach how to read the signs.

title: Gauss Map As A Spherical Sensor
notes: Stress that the Gauss map does not draw the original surface again; it records the direction of the oriented normal. A small patch whose normals rotate quickly sweeps a larger patch on the sphere, so area distortion becomes a curvature measurement.

title: Differentiating The Normal
notes: Explain the minus sign in the shape operator as a convention that aligns convex surfaces with positive principal curvatures for the outward normal. The derivative of the normal is tangent-valued because the normal has constant length, so all bending information returns to the tangent plane.

title: Shape Operator Ledger
notes: Present the shape operator as the linear map that compares how tangent directions change the normal. In coordinates it is obtained by raising an index of the second fundamental form with the first fundamental form, which separates metric measurement from normal acceleration.

title: Self-Adjoint Maps Have Orthogonal Axes
notes: This slide is the linear algebra hinge of the chapter. Because the shape operator is self-adjoint for the first fundamental form, its eigenvectors can be chosen orthogonal, and the surface receives two principal directions except at umbilic points.

title: Curvature Invariants
notes: Move from eigenvalues to invariant summaries. Gaussian curvature is the determinant of the shape operator and records signed area distortion of the Gauss map, while mean curvature is half the trace and records the average normal bending.

title: Sign Diagnostics
notes: Use the three panels as a visual taxonomy rather than a proof. Positive Gaussian curvature means both principal curvatures have the same sign, negative curvature means the surface bends in opposite senses, and zero curvature means one principal direction is locally flat to first order.

title: Dupin Indicatrix And Asymptotic Lines
notes: The Dupin indicatrix translates the quadratic normal curvature form into a plane picture. Elliptic points produce closed level curves, hyperbolic points produce crossed branches with asymptotic directions, and parabolic points sit at the boundary between these behaviors.

title: Graph Patch Curvature Ledger
notes: For a graph patch, the formulas expose what the notebook computations are checking. First derivatives control the metric denominator, second derivatives control normal acceleration, and at a critical point the Hessian eigenvalues directly become the principal curvatures.

title: Umbilics Collapse The Direction Field
notes: At an umbilic the shape operator is a scalar multiple of the identity, so every tangent direction is principal. The difficulty is not that curvature disappears, but that the principal-direction line field loses a preferred pair of axes and needs a separate local analysis.

title: Examples Calibrate The Formulas
notes: Compare the sphere, cylinder, saddle, and minimal-surface model as calibration tests. The same shape-operator ledger explains constant positive curvature, one zero principal curvature, opposite-sign curvatures, and vanishing mean curvature without requiring unrelated memorized cases or special notation.

title: Principal Directions Become Curves
notes: Once principal directions are found at each point, they form line fields that can be integrated where no degeneracy intervenes. Lines of curvature follow eigenvectors, while asymptotic lines follow directions of zero normal curvature on hyperbolic regions.

title: Notebook Diagnostics
notes: Connect the lecture deck back to reproducible computation. A curvature sensor should check normal length, tangent-valued derivatives, self-adjointness, eigenvalue agreement with trace and determinant, and stable sign classification under small coordinate perturbations before trusting any visual label.

title: Applied Lab
notes: Invite students to treat curvature as an instrument design problem. Given sampled graph data, estimate the first and second fundamental forms, symmetrize the shape operator with respect to the metric, and compare the resulting signs with geometric inspection of the mesh.

title: Recap
notes: Close by tracing the continuous story. The Gauss map measures normal rotation, the shape operator differentiates it inside the tangent plane, self-adjointness produces principal axes, and determinant, trace, and quadratic forms turn bending into diagnostics for points and curves.
